mainTopic: The three sins one may not commit even to save a life, healing with forbidden items, and the אביי–רבא dispute about forbidden benefit that comes against one's will.
overview: This amud finishes רבי יוחנן's rule that one may heal with anything forbidden except עבודה זרה, גילוי עריות and שפיכות דמים. The גמרא then gives a source for each exception. For עבודה זרה it points back to 'בכל נפשך'. For עריות, a ברייתא of רבי compares a נערה המאורסה to a רוצח. The comparison teaches that a רודף may be killed and that one must die rather than commit עריות. The rule for murder itself comes from סברא, shown by רבא's ruling: 'Who says your blood is redder?' Next comes a story: רבינא treated his daughter with ערלה olives, and he explained it either as a case of danger or as an unusual way of benefiting. The amud ends with a dispute between אביי and רבא about forbidden benefit that comes to a person against his will. The גמרא gives two versions of exactly which case they argue about, based on whether the benefit was avoidable and whether he intended it, and links each version to רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון.

steps.title: The third exception: bloodshed
steps.stepSummary: The last words of רבי יוחנן's rule: you may heal with anything except עבודה זרה, גילוי עריות, and שפיכות דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: ...and bloodshed.
steps.whatsHappening: These two words finish a statement that began on the previous amud. One may heal with anything forbidden except three sins, and the last of the three is שפיכות דמים (murder).
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the end of a list, not a new idea. The whole list says that even to save a life, a person may not commit these three sins. The rest of this passage explains where each exception comes from.

phrases.english: and bloodshed.
phrases.notes: The end of the list: one may heal with anything except עבודה זרה, גילוי עריות, and שפיכות דמים.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the statement earlier.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even to save a life, one may not use healing that involves עבודה זרה, גילוי עריות, or שפיכות דמים.

steps.title: The source for idolatry was already given
steps.stepSummary: Where do we learn the exception for עבודה זרה? From what was just said earlier.
steps.simpleTranslation: Idolatry: that is what we already said.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts listing sources for each of the three exceptions. For עבודה זרה, it simply points back to the source it already brought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא learned from 'בכל נפשך' (with all your soul) that one must give up his life rather than serve idols. So no new source is needed here. The real work is finding sources for the other two.

keyTerms.meaning: 'That which we said', pointing back to an earlier source.

phrases.english: Idolatry: that which we said.
phrases.notes: This points back to 'with all your soul' (בכל נפשך).

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הָא דַּאֲמַרַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the first of the three exceptions listed in step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is the פסוק 'בכל נפשך', already quoted.

steps.title: A ברייתא links murder to the betrothed girl
steps.stepSummary: For גילוי עריות and שפיכות דמים, the גמרא brings a ברייתא of רבי quoting the פסוק that compares a murderer to the case of a נערה המאורסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Forbidden relations and bloodshed: as it was taught in a ברייתא, רבי says: 'For as when a man rises against his neighbor and kills him, so is this matter.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the source for the other two exceptions. It quotes a פסוק about a betrothed girl who was attacked, which mentions murder.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is in the section about a נערה המאורסה attacked in the field. Suddenly it says her case is 'like' a man who kills his neighbor. This comparison will be the key to learning both laws.

keyTerms.meaning: 'As it was taught', introducing a ברייתא.

phrases.english: Forbidden relations and bloodshed:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quietly asking: where do we learn these two from?

phrases.english: as it was taught: Rabbi says:
"For as when a man rises against his neighbor
and kills him,
so is this matter."
phrases.notes: 'This matter' is the attack on the betrothed girl.

steps.triggerLanguage: גִּילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת וּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים דְּתַנְיָא רַבִּי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the source for עבודה זרה to the source for the other two exceptions.
steps.raayaObject: That one must die rather than commit גילוי עריות or שפיכות דמים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי on דברים 22:26.

steps.title: Why is murder mentioned here?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks what a murderer has to do with a betrothed girl.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does a murderer have to do with a betrothed girl?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא points out that the comparison seems out of place. The פסוק already said the girl is not guilty, so why bring in murder?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the comparison only meant 'she is innocent, like a murder victim', it would add nothing. So the question sets up the idea that the comparison must teach real laws.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What does this have to do with...?', asking why a comparison is made.
A betrothed young woman (after אירוסין, before נישואין).

phrases.english: And what does a murderer have to do
with a betrothed young woman?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מָה עִנְיַן רוֹצֵחַ אֵצֶל נַעֲרָה הַמְאוֹרָסָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the comparison in the פסוק just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the comparison between murder and the betrothed girl comes to teach.

steps.title: Murder learns from the betrothed girl: stop the pursuer
steps.stepSummary: The comparison works both ways. First, just as one may save the girl even by killing the attacker, one may save a murder victim by killing the murderer.
steps.simpleTranslation: This case comes to teach, and it turns out it also learns. The תורה compares the murderer to the betrothed girl. Just as with the betrothed girl, one may save her at the cost of the attacker's life, so too with a murderer, one may save the victim at the cost of the murderer's life.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers that murder is mentioned in order to teach, and also to learn. Here it shows the first direction: murder learns the rule of רודף from the betrothed girl.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A היקש can go both ways. This step is the direction where murder learns from the girl's case. Anyone may stop someone chasing to kill, even by killing him.

keyTerms.meaning: It comes to teach and turns out to learn too: a two-way comparison.
Compares (a הֶקֵּשׁ, linking two cases in the פסוק).
One may save him at the cost of the pursuer's life (דין רוֹדֵף).

steps.confusionAlert: 'בנפשו' here means the attacker's life, not the victim's. We save the victim by killing the attacker.

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי זֶה בָּא לְלַמֵּד, וְנִמְצָא לָמֵד.
phrases.english: This comes to teach, and turns out to learn.
It compares a murderer to a betrothed young woman:
just as with a betrothed young woman,
one may save her at the cost of his [the attacker's] life,
so too with a murderer,
one may save him [the victim] at the cost of his [the murderer's] life.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲרֵי זֶה בָּא לְלַמֵּד וְנִמְצָא לָמֵד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why murder is mentioned: it is a two-way comparison.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Murder learns from the girl's case that one may kill a pursuer to save the victim.

steps.title: The betrothed girl learns from murder: die rather than sin
steps.stepSummary: The second direction: just as one must die rather than murder, a betrothed girl (and so all עריות) must die rather than sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the betrothed girl learns from the murderer. Just as with a murderer, one must be killed rather than transgress, so too a betrothed girl must be killed rather than transgress.
steps.whatsHappening: Now the comparison goes the other way. The girl's case learns from murder, and this gives our source for גילוי עריות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know (step 7–9 will explain how) that one may not kill another to save himself. Through the היקש, the same rule of יהרג ואל יעבור applies to עריות. This finishes the source for the second exception in step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him be killed rather than transgress.

steps.whatToRemember: The היקש of רוצח and נערה המאורסה teaches two laws: the רודף may be killed, and one must die rather than commit עריות, just as with murder.

phrases.english: And the betrothed young woman from the murderer:
just as with a murderer, one should be killed and not transgress,
so too a betrothed young woman,
she should be killed and not transgress.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנַעֲרָה הַמְאוֹרָסָה מֵרוֹצֵחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second direction of the same comparison.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: גילוי עריות carries יהרג ואל יעבור, learned from murder.

steps.title: Where does the rule for murder itself come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: we learned עריות from murder, but how do we know murder itself is יהרג ואל יעבור?
steps.simpleTranslation: And bloodshed itself, from where do we know it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that step 6 assumed murder is יהרג ואל יעבור. Now it asks what the source for that is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole היקש depends on knowing the rule for murder first. Without a source for murder, the rule for עריות has nothing to stand on.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know it?

phrases.english: And bloodshed itself, from where do we derive it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים גּוּפֵיהּ מְנָלַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the assumption that step 6 relied on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that murder is יהרג ואל יעבור.

steps.title: It is simple logic
steps.stepSummary: The answer: no פסוק is needed. It is סברא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is logic.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the rule for murder comes from logic, not from a פסוק. It is about to explain that logic with a story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סברא is as strong as a פסוק. Here, the logic is that no one may decide that his life is worth more than another person's.

phrases.english: It is logic:

steps.triggerLanguage: סְבָרָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Murder is יהרג ואל יעבור because of סברא.

steps.title: רבא: who says your blood is redder?
steps.stepSummary: רבא tells a man ordered to kill or be killed that he must let himself be killed, because his blood is not redder than the other man's.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like the man who came before רבא and said: the local ruler told me, 'Go kill so-and-so, and if not, I will kill you.' רבא said to him: let them kill you, and do not kill. What makes you think your blood is redder? Perhaps that man's blood is redder.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows the סברא through a real case before רבא. A man was told to kill or be killed, and רבא told him he may not kill.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Killing the other man to save yourself means saying your life is worth more, and no one can know that. So you may not take his life to save your own, which is the meaning of יהרג ואל יעבור for murder.
steps.whatToRemember: Murder is יהרג ואל יעבור by סברא: 'מאי חזית דדמא דידך סומק טפי'. Through the היקש, the same rule goes to עריות.
steps.whyThisMatters: This סברא is the basis in הלכה for never killing an innocent person to save oneself.

phrases.english: Like that man who came before Rava,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מָרֵי דּוּרַאי אֲמַר לִי:
phrases.english: he said to him: The local ruler said to me:
Go kill so-and-so,
and if not, I will kill you.
He said to him: Let them kill you, and do not kill.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי חָזֵית דִּדְמָא דִידָךְ סוּמָּק טְפֵי?
phrases.english: What did you see that your blood is redder?

phrases.aramaic: דִּילְמָא דְּמָא דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא סוּמָּק טְפֵי.
phrases.english: Perhaps that man's blood is redder.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָהוּא דַּאֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the סברא given in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: That murder is יהרג ואל יעבור by logic.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's ruling: 'מאי חזית דדמא דידך סומק טפי'.

steps.title: Treating a daughter with forbidden olives when there is no danger
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי finds רבינא rubbing his daughter with unripe ערלה olives. He challenges him: the חכמים allowed healing with forbidden things only when life is in danger, not otherwise.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי found רבינא rubbing his daughter with unripe olives of ערלה. He said to him: Fine, the חכמים said this is allowed when there is danger. But who said it is allowed when there is no danger?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story and then raises a challenge. רבינא is using forbidden ערלה fruit as medicine, and מר בר רב אשי questions whether this is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Benefit from ערלה is normally forbidden. The earlier rule allows healing with forbidden things when there is danger to life. מר בר רב אשי assumes the daughter was not in real danger, so he asks how רבינא could rely on that permission.

keyTerms.meaning: Fruit from a tree in its first three years; eating or benefiting from it is forbidden
A time of danger to life

phrases.aramaic: מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי אַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ לְרָבִינָא
phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi found Ravina
rubbing his daughter
with unripe olives of orlah.
He said to him: Say that the Sages said this
at a time of danger,
but when it is not a time of danger, who said it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימוֹר דַּאֲמוּר רַבָּנַן בִּשְׁעַת הַסַּכָּנָה, שֶׁלֹּא בִּשְׁעַת הַסַּכָּנָה מִי אֲמוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the discussion of יהרג ואל יעבור to a practical story about healing with a forbidden item.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's use of ערלה olives to treat his daughter
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The permission to heal with forbidden items applies only when there is danger; here there seems to be no danger.

steps.title: A high fever counts as danger
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that a burning fever is also treated like a time of danger.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This high fever is also considered like a time of danger.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא defends himself. He says his daughter's high fever is itself a dangerous situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא accepts the rule that permission requires danger. He only disagrees about the facts: a strong fever is serious enough to count as danger, so the permission applies.

keyTerms.meaning: Is similar to, is considered like

phrases.english: He said to him: This high fever
is also like a time of danger.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי אִישָּׁתָא צְמִירְתָּא נָמֵי כִּשְׁעַת הַסַּכָּנָה דָּמְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the situation really is one of danger
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A fever is not dangerous, so healing with ערלה would be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: A high fever counts as danger, so healing with a forbidden item is allowed.

steps.title: Second version: not the normal way of benefiting
steps.stepSummary: Another version says רבינא answered that he was not using the olives in the normal way people benefit from them, so it is allowed even without danger.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say he answered him: Am I benefiting in the normal way?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different version of רבינא's answer. Here he says the type of use itself is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The normal way to benefit from olives is to let them ripen and use their oil. Rubbing unripe olives on the skin is an unusual use. In this version, an unusual use of ערלה is permitted even when there is no danger, so the fever does not need to count as danger.

keyTerms.meaning: The normal way of benefiting from something

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a second answer added to the first one. It is a different report of what רבינא said. In this version he does not claim there was danger at all.

phrases.english: Some say he said to him:
Am I doing it in a normal way of benefit?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מִידֵּי דֶּרֶךְ הֲנָאָה קָא עָבֵידְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: An alternative version of the answer given in step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the prohibition: unusual use is not forbidden benefit
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any benefit from ערלה is forbidden unless there is danger.
steps.terutzMaskana: Using ערלה in an unusual way (שלא כדרך הנאתו) is allowed even without danger.
steps.whyThisMatters: It introduces the important idea that the prohibition of benefit targets normal use, not every unusual use.

steps.title: אביי and רבא argue about benefit that comes without one's choice
steps.stepSummary: A new dispute is brought: if forbidden benefit comes to a person against his will, אביי says it is allowed and רבא says it is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: Benefit that comes to a person against his will: אביי said it is permitted, and רבא said it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic connected to forbidden benefit. It quotes a disagreement between אביי and רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is benefit a person did not set out to get, but which reaches him anyway. אביי permits it and רבא forbids it. The next lines will explain exactly which case they are arguing about.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces a statement or dispute of the אמוראים)
Against his will, without his choosing it

phrases.aramaic: אִיתְּמַר: הֲנָאָה הַבָּאָה לוֹ לְאָדָם בְּעַל כׇּרְחוֹ,
phrases.english: It was stated: Benefit that comes to a person against his will,
Abaye said: It is permitted,
and Rava said: It is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: הֲנָאָה הַבָּאָה לוֹ לְאָדָם בְּעַל כׇּרְחוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the story to a general dispute about forbidden benefit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי: unwanted benefit from a forbidden item is permitted. רבא: it is forbidden.

steps.title: The cases where everyone agrees
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains: if the person intends to benefit, everyone forbids it, whether or not he could avoid it. If he cannot avoid it and does not intend it, everyone permits it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he could avoid it and he intends to benefit, or if he could not avoid it and he intends to benefit, everyone agrees it is forbidden. If he could not avoid it and he does not intend to benefit, everyone agrees it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the dispute by listing the cases that are not argued about. This sets up the next line, which will name the one case that is disputed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two questions matter: could he avoid the benefit (אפשר), and does he want it (מיכוין)? If he wants it, it is always forbidden. If he cannot avoid it and does not want it, it is always permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: It is possible (to avoid the benefit)
Everyone agrees, there is no dispute

steps.confusionAlert: Here אפשר does not mean 'maybe.' It means it was possible for him to avoid the benefit.

phrases.english: Where it is possible to avoid and he intends,
or it is not possible to avoid and he intends —
everyone agrees that it is forbidden.
Where it is not possible to avoid and he does not intend —
everyone agrees that it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶפְשָׁר וְקָא מִיכַּוֵּין, לָא אֶפְשָׁר וְקָמִיכַּוֵין, כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דְּאָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the scope of the dispute stated in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Intent to benefit always forbids. Unavoidable and unintended benefit is always permitted.

steps.title: The one case they argue about
steps.stepSummary: The real dispute between אביי and רבא is where the person could avoid the benefit but does not intend it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where they disagree is where it is possible to avoid it and he does not intend to benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the exact case of the dispute. This finishes the explanation of what אביי and רבא are arguing about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Of the four combinations, three are agreed upon. The only disputed one is where he could have avoided the benefit but did not want it. אביי permits because he lacks intent. רבא forbids because he could have avoided it.
steps.whatToRemember: Four cases: intends benefit means forbidden (everyone). Cannot avoid and does not intend means permitted (everyone). Can avoid but does not intend is the dispute: אביי permits, רבא forbids.

phrases.english: Where they disagree is where it is possible to avoid and he does not intend.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי דְּאֶפְשָׁר וְלָא מִיכַּוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the clarification begun in step 14 by naming the disputed case.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The אביי and רבא dispute applies only where the benefit was avoidable but unintended.

steps.title: According to רבי יהודה, everyone forbids
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא narrows the dispute further. According to רבי יהודה, who forbids an unintended act, both אביי and רבא agree that the benefit is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי יהודה, who said that an act done without intent is forbidden, everyone agrees that it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is shrinking the dispute even more. It says that if we follow רבי יהודה, nobody argues: the benefit is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that a forbidden result is forbidden even if you did not intend it (דבר שאין מתכוין אסור). Our case is 'possible to avoid, but no intent.' Under רבי יהודה's rule, the lack of intent does not help, so both אביי and רבא must forbid it.

keyTerms.meaning: An act whose forbidden result the person does not intend
Everyone agrees (literally: the whole world does not argue)

steps.confusionAlert: דבר שאין מתכוין is not the same as 'against his will' in general. It refers specifically to someone who does a permitted action, and a forbidden result happens without his intent. The גמרא is borrowing this famous concept to explain our case.

phrases.english: And according to Rabbi Yehuda,
who said: an unintended act is forbidden —
everyone agrees that it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, דְּאָמַר: דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Further narrows the case defined in Step 15 (possible to avoid, no intent) by tying it to רבי יהודה's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, both אביי and רבא forbid benefit that could be avoided, even without intent.

steps.title: The dispute exists only according to רבי שמעון, and אביי follows him
steps.stepSummary: The real dispute is according to רבי שמעון, who permits an unintended act. אביי follows רבי שמעון straightforwardly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where they argue is according to רבי שמעון, who said that an act done without intent is permitted. אביי holds like רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the argument only exists if we follow רבי שמעון. It explains that אביי simply follows רבי שמעון's rule, and this sets up how רבא will read רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון says lack of intent makes an act permitted. אביי applies this directly: since the person did not intend the benefit, it is allowed, even though he could have avoided it.

phrases.english: Where they argue is according to Rabbi Shimon,
who said: an unintended act is permitted.
Abaye holds like Rabbi Shimon,

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having removed רבי יהודה's view from the dispute, the גמרא places the dispute within רבי שמעון's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי permits avoidable but unintended benefit, following רבי שמעון's rule that דבר שאין מתכוין is מותר.

steps.title: רבא limits רבי שמעון's leniency to unavoidable cases
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that רבי שמעון only permitted an unintended act when it was impossible to avoid. Where it could be avoided, even רבי שמעון forbids.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא says: רבי שמעון only said this where it is impossible to avoid. But where it is possible to avoid, he did not say it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains how he can forbid the benefit even according to רבי שמעון. He reads רבי שמעון's leniency narrowly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without this, it would look like רבא is simply disagreeing with רבי שמעון. רבא answers that רבי שמעון's rule only covers situations where the person had no way out. Our case, where the benefit could be avoided, falls outside that rule, so it stays forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: He only said his ruling up to this point (a formula that limits someone's ruling)

steps.whatToRemember: Version 1: According to רבי יהודה, everyone forbids. According to רבי שמעון, אביי permits. רבא says רבי שמעון permits only when it is impossible to avoid.

phrases.aramaic: וְרָבָא אָמַר: עַד כָּאן לָא קָא אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן —
phrases.english: And Rava says: Rabbi Shimon only said this —
in a case where it is impossible to avoid,
but where it is possible to avoid — no.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָבָא אָמַר: עַד כָּאן לָא קָא אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the implied problem: how can רבא forbid, given רבי שמעון's leniency?
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of an earlier authority's ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי שמעון permits every unintended act, so רבא seems to contradict him.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי שמעון's leniency applies only where avoidance was impossible, so רבא can forbid avoidable benefit even according to רבי שמעון.

steps.title: Second version: mapping the cases differently
steps.stepSummary: A second version says the case of 'possible to avoid, no intent' is just the old רבי יהודה / רבי שמעון dispute. The case of 'impossible to avoid, no intent' is permitted by everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: Where it is possible to avoid and he does not intend, that is exactly the dispute of רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון. Where it is impossible to avoid and he does not intend, everyone agrees it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different version (איכא דאמרי) of how to understand the dispute of אביי and רבא. It first clears away the cases they cannot be arguing about, which sets up where their real dispute is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, אביי and רבא would not be arguing about 'possible and no intent,' because that is already the famous dispute between רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון. They also do not argue about 'impossible and no intent,' since everyone permits it. This leaves only one case, which the next step names.
steps.confusionAlert: Notice that this version reverses Step 15. There, 'possible to avoid, no intent' was the case of אביי and רבא. Here, that same case is said to belong to רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון instead.

phrases.english: Some say: possible to avoid and he does not intend —

phrases.aramaic: הַיְינוּ פְּלוּגְתַּיְיהוּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן.
phrases.english: that is the dispute of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.
Impossible to avoid and he does not intend —
everyone agrees that it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אֶפְשָׁר וְלָא מִיכַּוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative version that replaces the case mapping of Steps 14 through 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Possible and unintended belongs to the רבי יהודה / רבי שמעון dispute. Impossible and unintended is permitted by all.

steps.title: The dispute is where it is unavoidable but he intends
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, אביי and רבא argue about a case where the benefit could not be avoided, but the person does want it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where they argue is where it is impossible to avoid, and he does intend to benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the one remaining case in this second version. That is where אביי and רבא disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The benefit is coming no matter what, but the person is glad to get it. The question is whether his intent alone makes it forbidden, even though he could not have avoided it.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי פְּלִיגִי, דְּלָא אֶפְשָׁר וְקָא מִיכַּוֵּין.
phrases.english: Where they argue is where it is impossible to avoid and he intends.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי, דְּלָא אֶפְשָׁר וְקָא מִיכַּוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from Step 19's elimination of the other cases.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In version 2, the dispute is 'impossible to avoid, but he intends.'

steps.title: According to רבי שמעון, intent forbids for everyone
steps.stepSummary: Since רבי שמעון makes the law depend on intent, both אביי and רבא agree that intended benefit is forbidden according to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי שמעון, who follows intent, everyone agrees that it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows this second version further. It shows that according to רבי שמעון, nobody argues.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי שמעון, intent is the deciding factor. If the person intends the benefit, it is forbidden, even if avoiding it was impossible.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן דְּאָזֵיל בָּתַר כַּוּוֹנָה —
phrases.english: And according to Rabbi Shimon, who goes after intent —
everyone agrees that it is forbidden,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן דְּאָזֵיל בָּתַר כַּוּוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors Step 16, but now with רבי שמעון as the opinion under which there is no dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי שמעון, intended benefit is forbidden even if unavoidable.

steps.title: The dispute is according to רבי יהודה, who looks only at avoidability
steps.stepSummary: אביי and רבא argue according to רבי יהודה, who ignores intent and asks only whether the benefit could be avoided.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where they argue is according to רבי יהודה, who said: it makes no difference whether one intends or does not intend. If it is possible to avoid, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא places the dispute within רבי יהודה's view. This sets up which side אביי takes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה's test is avoidability, not intent. That implies that an unavoidable case would be permitted even with intent. The question is whether to follow that implication fully.

phrases.english: Where they argue is according to Rabbi Yehuda,
who said: no difference whether he intends
or does not intend,
if it is possible to avoid, it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, דְּאָמַר: לָא שְׁנָא מִתְכַּוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels Step 17, now placing the dispute under רבי יהודה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For רבי יהודה, avoidability alone decides. Intent is irrelevant.

steps.title: אביי follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, אביי follows רבי יהודה. Since the benefit was unavoidable, it is permitted even with intent.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי holds like רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us אביי's position in the second version. He applies רבי יהודה's avoidability test fully.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because רבי יהודה ignores intent and forbids only what could be avoided, אביי permits the unavoidable case even when the person wants the benefit.
steps.whatToRemember: Version 2: Possible and unintended is the רבי יהודה / רבי שמעון dispute. Impossible and unintended is permitted by all. Impossible and intended is the dispute: according to רבי שמעון it is forbidden by all, and according to רבי יהודה, אביי permits it.

phrases.english: Abaye holds like Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּיֵי כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Assigns אביי to רבי יהודה's view, as described in Step 22.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In version 2, אביי permits unavoidable benefit even when intended, following רבי יהודה's avoidability test.
